items.headline: Israeli opposition accuses Netanyahu of trying to 'delegitimise' election
items.blurb: The PM's Likud party has alleged foreign interference and said Arab-led parties "stole" the election after his coalition lost its majority.
items.text: The main Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot and Arab-led party leaders have denounced Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for alleging foreign interference following the election which saw his coalition lose its majority. Netanyahu's Likud accused Israel's Arab-led parties of "stealing" the election. Home security agency Shin Bet is investigating whether they received illegal funding from Qatar and Turkey. Qatar's foreign ministry denied the "ridiculous and dangerous" allegations and accused Israeli politicians of conducting a disinformation campaign against Doha. Final results confirmed that neither Netanyahu's bloc nor the Jewish opposition had won a majority in parliament. The two Arab party lists - The Joint List and the Ra'am - defied expectations to win a record 19 seats in the 120-seat Knesset following a surge in turnout among Arab voters. That positions them as potential kingmakers, with Netanyahu's bloc winning 53 seats and his rival Gadi Eisenkot's bloc securing 48. items.headline: Trump administration renews bid to block Alaska election results
items.blurb: The updated lawsuit cites a new report that Democratic operatives recruited a competitor to confuse voters.
items.text: The United States Department of Justice has filed a revised lawsuit seeking to decertify the results of a Senate race in the state of Alaska if Republican incumbent Dan S Sullivan loses narrowly. The updated lawsuit on Thursday comes just days before the November 3 midterm election , which will determine control of Congress. The complaint accuses Democrats of trying to confuse voters by placing a candidate with the same name as Sullivan on the ballot. Alaska’s Senate race is one of seven key toss-ups that will likely decide whether Republicans keep their majority in Congress’s upper chamber. Democratic challenger Mary Peltola is seeking to unseat Sullivan, a Republican ally of US President Donald Trump. But a New York Times report on Wednesday alleged that members of Peltola’s campaign helped recruit a retired teacher, Dan J Sullivan Jr, to run for the Senate seat as a spoiler candidate, designed to draw votes away from the incumbent. The Times report prompted a renewed legal push under the Trump administration to bar Alaska from certifying its election results, should Senator Sullivan lose.

items.blurb: Warnings of escalating clampdown on press freedom come after Cairo court convicts Attalah of managing an unlicensed website Lina Attalah, a prominent Egyptian journalist and the editor-in-chief of the news outlet Mada Masr, has been released from detention by Egypt’s authorities and had her website ordered to be shut…
items.text: Warnings of escalating clampdown on press freedom come after Cairo court convicts Attalah of managing an unlicensed website Lina Attalah, a prominent Egyptian journalist and the editor-in-chief of the news outlet Mada Masr, has been released from detention by Egypt’s authorities and had her website ordered to be shut down by a court amid an intensifying crackdown on independent media in the country. Attalah was taken briefly into custody after a Cairo court convicted her of managing an unlicensed website, prompting fresh international concerns over press freedom in Egypt. According to Mada Masr, Attalah was released after the news outlet had paid a fine of 3m Egyptian pounds ($53,500; £40,100), prompting statements of support from global human rights groups. “Lina Attalah was released after we paid the said fine,” said her lawyer Hassan al-Azhari. “In the process, we discovered that she had been sentenced in absentia in 2024 to a year in prison, as well as a fine of 20,000 Egyptian pounds,” he told AFP. items.headline: Audio reveals exchanges between Spain train operators and drivers moments before deadly crash
items.blurb: The leaked tapes appear to show one high-speed train was given clearance to move at normal speed, even though another up ahead had stalled.
items.text: Leaked audio recordings that were published in Spanish media have revealed conversations between train drivers and a control centre just minutes before a deadly crash on Wednesday morning, that has killed 69 people. Officials are investigating the cause of the disaster, which occurred when a train from Madrid to Seville barrelled into a stationary train near Urda. Three audio recordings between Madrid's control centre and two train drivers appear to show that one high-speed train was given clearance to move even though another train had stalled on the track, about 25km (15 miles) ahead. Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has said that authorities will "get to the bottom of every last detail of this tragedy". Dozens of people were injured, with survivors recounting harrowing scenes people crying and bleeding, passengers trapped in their seats, missing limbs and smoke billowing throughout the carriages, one of which caught fire. On Thursday, Spain's King Felipe VI and Queen Letizia visited some of the injured passengers in a hospital in Toledo. items.headline: 'The city is alive': A brief peace in Kherson, but residents fear what comes next
items.blurb: A temporary ceasefire has brought rare quiet to Kherson, offering its residents a glimpse of normal life before fighting resumes.
items.text: The Ukrainian city of Kherson has known its first two days of quiet after many years, as a US-brokered temporary ceasefire has allowed residents rare moments of respite from the constant Russian aerial attacks that plague the front line region. Videos posted on social media showed people strolling down streets covered in anti-drone nets and gathering in the city's squares - ordinary activities that usually mean keeping one eye on the sky and one ear out for incoming drones. "Ever since the ceasefire was announced, there's been total silence," said Olga, 42, speaking by phone from Kherson. "We are all, of course, overjoyed." "I don't even know what to call it," she added, her smile coming through in her voice. "It's as if everything has finally come to an end." Since Tuesday, Kherson has "literally come back to life," Ukraine's human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said. "People are calmly going out, walking, enjoying the autumn sun. items.headline: EU force helicopter crash kills four in Bosnia
items.blurb: EUFOR confirms CH-47 Chinook helicopter crash in Bosnia, with four Italian nationals confirmed dead.
items.text: Four people belonging to the European Union Force in Bosnia ( EUFOR ) have been killed after an Italian military helicopter conducting a training operation crashed. EUFOR said a CH-47 Chinook helicopter crashed during “routine training” in the Brcko region on Thursday, about 180km (110 miles) north of Bosnia’s capital, Sarajevo. A total of 11 people were injured in the crash, EUFOR said, adding that all the injured are receiving treatment and are in stable condition. The Italian government said in a statement that all those on board the military helicopter were its nationals. The victims were two soldiers and two Red Cross volunteers, according to the Italian defence ministry. “At this moment of immense grief, my thoughts go first and foremost to the families of our fallen, to whom I extend my personal condolences and those of the entire defence establishment,” Italian Defence Minister Guido Crosetto said. A year after the fall of El Fasher , the British government said it had sanctioned military leaders from both sides in the country’s ongoing conflict whom it suspected of sexual violence during the siege of the city. A total of 15 commanders from the military groups – the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) – have been subjected to a travel ban and an asset freeze . The Foreign Office said it hoped the action would ensure “the horrors that took place at El Fasher will be known to the world”. items.headline: Russian drone attack on Ukrainian train station kills at least 14, officials say
items.blurb: At least 14 others were wounded in the attack in the central city of Dnipro, including an 11-year-old boy.
items.text: At least 14 people have been killed after a Russian jet-powered drone hit a crowded platform at the main railway station in the central Ukrainian city of Dnipro, local officials have said. Dnipropetrovsk regional head Oleksandr Hanzha said at least 14 others were wounded in the attack, including an 11-year-old boy. Ukraine's state railway operator, Ukrzaliznytsia, said a passenger train headed for the southern city of Zaporizhzhia was at one of the platforms in Dnipro when the drone hit. Russia's military has not publicly commented. It has repeatedly hit Ukraine's large railway network, but Moscow denies deliberately targeting civilians. In Dnipro, an elevated threat level was announced ahead of Thursday's strike, according to the railway operator chief, Oleksandr Pertsovsky. "But unfortunately there were still a large number of people on the platform" when the drone struck, he said. Dnipro Mayor Borys Filatov said the incident was a tragedy, adding that a drone hit an electric civilian train. items.blurb: In nearly seven months between April 2 and October 29, the board has issued multiple circulars, notifications and clarifications, including successive changes to its three-language policy
items.text: The dropping of three planned curricular components for students currently in Class 9 on Thursday is the latest in a series of changes to the Central Board of Secondary Education’s (CBSE) scheme of studies since the 2026–27 academic year began on April 1. In nearly seven months between April 2 and October 29, the board has issued multiple circulars, notifications and clarifications, including successive changes to its three-language policy introduced in line with the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020. The latest move came six days after the National Council of Educational Research and Training (NCERT) released a 20-hour introductory module on computational thinking (CT) and artificial intelligence (AI) for Classes 9 to 12 on October 23. In a circular dated October 29, CBSE said Individuals in Society and the CT and AI modules would not be part of the Class 9 curriculum in 2026–27, while Environmental Education would be excluded when the same batch moves to Class 10 in 2027–28. items.blurb: The revisions follow requests from the Chief Electoral Officers of the concerned States
items.text: The poll panel wrote separately to the five States and the Union Territory of Delhi about extending the timelines. File | Photo Credit: Allen Egenuse. J The Election Commission of India (ECI) on Thursday (October 29, 2026) revised the schedule for the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls in Maharashtra, Delhi, Andhra Pradesh, Haryana, Telangana, and Nagaland. The revisions follow requests from the Chief Electoral Officers of the concerned States. The poll panel wrote separately to the five States and the Union Territory of Delhi about extending the timelines. In Maharashtra, the deadline for filing claims and objections has been extended from October 26 to November 13. The notice phase and disposal of claims will now run until November 25, and the final roll will be published on November 30. The draft roll came out on August 31, and disposals had previously been fixed for November 10. In Delhi, claims and objections can now be filed until November 25, instead of October 30. items.headline: Fresh rules issued for dredging in forest areas to mitigate floods
items.blurb: The Centre has issued fresh guidelines allowing scientifically planned river dredging in forest areas to mitigate floods and restore river ecosystems, without treating the activity as a “non-forest purpose” and exempting qualifying works from forest clearance requirements, compensatory afforestation and net present…
items.text: The Centre has issued fresh guidelines allowing scientifically planned river dredging in forest areas to mitigate floods and restore river ecosystems, without treating the activity as a “non-forest purpose” and exempting qualifying works from forest clearance requirements, compensatory afforestation and net present value (NPV) payments. The guidelines come following Himachal Pradesh chief minister Sukhvinder Singh Sukhu’s meeting with Union environment minister Bhupender Yadav in September, where he sought a separate framework for dredging in flood-affected rivers. Sukhu had cited the accumulation of debris, silt, stones and boulders after extreme rainfall and flash floods, which narrows river channels and reduces their water-carrying capacity. The guidelines, dated October 27, clarify that scientific, planned and time-bound dredging to remove material accumulated due to natural disasters or extreme weather, restore river flow and protect forest ecosystems would not be treated as a non-forest purpose, provided the prescribed conditions are met. However, the ministry has set conditions to prevent the provision from being used to facilitate commercial extraction. items.blurb: IndiGo CEO Willie Walsh on Thursday indicated that higher ticket prices were unavoidable after the airline reported a net loss of ₹1,879 crore in the September quarter mainly due to pressure from elevated jet fuel prices and the depreciation of the rupee
items.text: IndiGo CEO Willie Walsh on Thursday indicated that higher ticket prices were unavoidable after the airline reported a net loss of ₹ 1,879 crore in the September quarter mainly due to pressure from elevated jet fuel prices and the depreciation of the rupee. The loss narrowed from ₹ 2,582 crore in the year-ago quarter but the airline’s fuel bill rose 67.2% year-on-year to nearly ₹ 9,967 crore, even as revenue from operations increased 25.9% to ₹ 23,364 crore. Walsh, who took over as CEO in August, said despite raising fares and adding fuel surcharges, the airline had been able to recover only about 60% of the increase in the fuel bill. Walsh said IndiGo would have to consider raising fares further to offset the rise, while trying to limit the impact on passengers. items.blurb: Backed by an ₹86 crore government grant and ₹70 crore Series A funding, Peptris Technologies is leveraging generative AI to build a preclinical pipeline targeting rare diseases and previously undruggable proteins.
items.text: Mumbai: In the mid-2010s, a scientist and a software engineer met through their children, frequently running into each other outside birthday parties and school events. Conversations fixated on what was new in their professional worlds: drug discovery for Shridhar Narayanan, former head of research and development (R&D) at AstraZeneca’s Bengaluru lab, and machine learning for software engineer Venkatasubramanian Narayanan, known better as just Venkat. These casual interactions eventually evolved into serious discussions on how technology and artificial intelligence (AI) could intersect with drug discovery, culminating in the establishment of an AI-driven drug discovery platform. The goal was to leverage AI to accelerate discovery timelines while targeting hard-to-treat diseases with significant unmet medical needs. Founded in 2019, Peptris Technologies was incubated at the sprawling Centre for Cellular and Molecular Platforms (C-CAMP) campus in Bengaluru. Its proprietary AI platform accelerates the discovery of potential molecules ready for wet-lab testing and expands the scope of diseases and drug targets for which candidate molecules can be identified. items.blurb: GIFT Nifty futures were at 22,981 as of 7:42 a.m. IST, indicating a positive start for the benchmark Nifty 50, which closed at 22,936.75 on Thursday.
items.text: Indian shares are set to open marginally higher on Friday, after upbeat earnings aided a rebound in the previous session, though higher crude oil prices are likely to limit follow-through gains. GIFT Nifty futures were at 22,981 as of 7:42 a.m. IST, indicating a positive start for the benchmark Nifty 50, which closed at 22,936.75 on Thursday. Both the benchmarks Nifty and BSE Sensex gained over 1% each in the previous session, after strong quarterly results from key constituents and as the US Federal Reserve held interest rates steady as expected. They have gained about 1.4% and 2.3%, respectively, in October, on course to snap a two-month selling streak, with sentiment finding some support from expectations of a potential review of long-term capital gains tax and steady corporate earnings despite global headwinds, said analysts at Geojit Investments and Equinomics Research. "Overall market bias has improved to cautiously positive, supported by the breakout from recent consolidation and broad-based sector buying, though elevated crude prices remains an important risk," said Hitesh Tailor, technical research analyst at Choice Broking. items.blurb: The firm has not said how much was potentially stolen but some crypto experts have put the figure at over $5bn.
items.text: Cryptocurrency giant Binance said on Thursday that it has frozen digital assets worth around $3bn (£2.24bn) to prevent them from being stolen while it investigates a security issue. The company said as part of a series of alerts online that all deposits and withdrawals are temporarily suspended while its teams conduct security checks and that the firm will "cover all losses". "It does look like a hack on Binance," said Binance's former boss Changpeng Zhao, who remains a majority shareholder of the firm. Two other major crypto platforms, Tether and Circle, said they have also frozen a total of about $2.4bn of assets in response to the potential Binance hack. Binance said the amount of funds frozen may continue to increase as its teams work closely with law enforcement and other partners to trace and seize additional assets. "We are working around the clock and will share a full post-mortem once the investigation is complete. items.blurb: An ED investigation into alleged foreign exchange violations involving crypto transfers above ₹4,900 crore has brought Mudrex and Instadapp under scrutiny.
items.text: The Enforcement Directorate (ED) on Thursday said it had conducted searches in Karnataka and Madhya Pradesh as part of an investigation into alleged foreign exchange violations involving cross-border cryptocurrency transfers worth more than ₹ 4,900 crore. The searches were carried out on October 26 under the Foreign Exchange Management Act ( FEMA ). The operation covered three premises in Bengaluru and one in Madhya Pradesh, the federal agency said in a statement. "Preliminary findings during the investigation revealed contravention of FEMA through unauthorised cross-border money transfer, unauthorised crypto balances in foreign platforms amounting to more than ₹ 4600 crore," the statement said. According to the ED, the searches revealed the alleged misuse of crypto tokens for unauthorised cross-border money transfers and financial transactions, including transactions involving certain tax-haven jurisdictions. The investigation has brought cryptocurrency platform Mudrex and decentralised finance platform Instadapp under scrutiny over their alleged roles in transactions that may have violated foreign exchange regulations. Around the same time, another OpenAI agent accessed private files from an Australian government website. It’s a problem that’s by no means confined to OpenAI. In the months since, Anthropic, Google, and Meta have also disclosed incidents in which their agents have gone off track. And worryingly, in many cases the agents eluded the very researchers and safety teams tasked with monitoring them. items.headline: Creating AI value with enterprise context
items.blurb: Across a business, any number of AI platforms, systems, and tools may be at work simultaneously—for example, AI-powered customer platforms, conversational assistants, and workflow and process automation tools. Each one is sophisticated, advanced, and quick to respond.
items.text: Across a business, any number of AI platforms, systems, and tools may be at work simultaneously—for example, AI-powered customer platforms, conversational assistants, and workflow and process automation tools. Each one is sophisticated, advanced, and quick to respond. But, when set to work, the outcomes and actions that emerge may be wrong, confused, or lacking a proper understanding of the business. Many organizations find themselves in this situation—and it could be one of key reasons they struggle to extract returns on their AI investments. An MIT Technology Review Insights poll finds that while every organization surveyed is using AI today to some degree, fewer than one in five (16%) are extracting transformative value from their deployments. The largest percentage of respondents (40%) say they are seeing moderate gains in specific tasks or teams, while 21% report meaningful gains, leaving 23% that are seeing minimal returns or none at all.
